title: Finding the eigenvectors
summary: For each eigenvalue of B, solve (B − λI)v = 0 for a direction, check Bv = λv by hand, and see they are not perpendicular.

blocks.title: B − 5I
blocks.why: An eigenvector for $\lambda$ is a non-zero solution of $(B - \lambda I)\,v = 0$. First write the matrix down.

slips.say: $5I$ is 5 on the diagonal only. The off-diagonal entries of $B$ stay.

hints: Take 5 off each diagonal entry. Leave the others alone.

check.say: Its determinant must be 0, because 5 is an eigenvalue. If it is not, look for a slip before going on.

blocks.solution: Row 2 is $-2$ times row 1. That is what a zero determinant looks like: the two rows give one equation, not two.

blocks.title: The eigenvector for 5
blocks.why: Solving $(B - 5I)\,v = 0$ gives the line that $B$ stretches by 5.

answer.acceptNote: Any non-zero multiple is right: it is the same line, and the course writes it as $(1, 1)$.

slips.say: $(0, 0)$ solves it, but the zero vector is never an eigenvector. Pick $x = 1$ and find $y$.

hints: Write $v = (x, y)$. Row 1 of the matrix gives one equation in $x$ and $y$.
Row 1: $-x + y = 0$. Row 2, $2x - 2y = 0$, says the same thing.

check.say: $B$ times your $v$ should be $5v$. With $B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$, each row of $B$ dotted with $v$ should be 5 times that entry of $v$.

blocks.solution: $(1, 1)$: $B\,(1, 1) = (5, 5)$. Every point on the line $y = x$ is an eigenvector for 5.

blocks.title: The eigenvector for 2
blocks.why: Each eigenvalue has its own line of eigenvectors. Same method, other eigenvalue.
blocks.prompt: $B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 2. Solve $(B - 2I)\,v = 0$ for a non-zero $v$. Take the one with first entry 1.

answer.acceptNote: Any non-zero multiple is right: it is the same line. The course writes it as $(1, -2)$.

slips.say: $x$ and $y$ swapped: $2x + y = 0$ gives $y = -2x$, so with $x = 1$, $y = -2$.

hints: First write out $B - 2I$: take 2 off each diagonal entry.
$B - 2I = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$. Both rows give the same equation.

check.say: Put your $v$ into $2x + y$: it should give 0.

blocks.solution: $(1, -2)$, the line $y = -2x$. Next, check it the direct way.

blocks.title: Check Bv = 2v
blocks.why: The direct check catches a slip in any earlier step: if $Bv$ is not $\lambda v$, something went wrong.

slips.say: That is $B^\mathsf{T}(1, -2)$: you used the columns of $B$ as rows. Row 1 of $B$ is $(4, 1)$.
That is $B\,(1, 2)$. The second entry of the vector is $-2$.

hints: Each entry is a row of $B$ dotted with $(1, -2)$.

check.say: If $(1, -2)$ is an eigenvector for 2, the answer is $2\,(1, -2)$.

blocks.title: Another eigenvector for 2
blocks.why: An eigenvector is a line, so it can look different from the one you found. This checks you can spot it.
blocks.prompt: $B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 5 and 2. Which of these is an eigenvector for $\lambda = 2$?

options.say: Not this one: a sign slip. $B\,(1, 2) = (6, 8)$, not a multiple of $(1, 2)$. The line is $y = -2x$.
Not this one. It is an eigenvector, but for 5: $B\,(1, 1) = (5, 5)$.

blocks.hint: Is it a multiple of $(1, -2)$? Or multiply it by $B$.
blocks.solution: Every non-zero multiple of $(1, -2)$ is an eigenvector for 2, negative multiples included.

blocks.title: Are they perpendicular?
blocks.why: Next lesson needs eigenvectors that meet at a right angle. Test whether $B$'s do.
blocks.prompt: The eigenvectors of $B$ are $(1, 1)$ for 5 and $(1, -2)$ for 2. Compute $(1, 1) \cdot (1, -2)$.

slips.say: $1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-2)$ is not 0. Add the two products again.

hints: Multiply entry by entry, then add.

check.say: Perpendicular vectors have dot product 0. Sketch the lines $y = x$ and $y = -2x$: is the angle between them a right angle?

blocks.solution: $-1 \ne 0$, so they are not perpendicular. $B$ is not symmetric (its 1 and 2 differ). Next lesson: for a symmetric matrix they always are, and that is what the SVD uses.
